# TUI — Tables

### Rule 106 : Table standardization

- Use `theme.DefaultTableStyles()` for all tables
- Bold headers with ColorSecondary (see Rule 118)
- Selected row with ColorHighlight
- Consistent borders

### Rule 116 : the rendered row occupies exactly the inside of the viewport

**The selected row must extend all the way to the viewport's right border.**

The calculation belongs to `internal/ui/datatable`, and to it alone. A view
passes the **full viewport width, borders included** — `Resize` strips out
the borders and the padding `bubbles/table` adds per cell (`Padding(0, 1)`,
i.e. +2 per rendered column).

```go
func (m *Model) resize(width, height int) {
    m.table.Resize(width, max(height-1, 1)) // no -2, no max(…, 20)
}
```

Subtracting the borders a second time is the rule's most discreet defect:
the table is then correct at *every* width and also ends two cells too soon
at every one of them. A local floor (`max(…, 20)`) is the mirror-image
mistake — it makes the table wider than the viewport when the terminal is
narrow, which is exactly the forbidden overflow.

#### The invariant is stated over the **rendered** extent

```go
// ✅ CORRECT
if got, want := m.table.RenderedWidth(), width-2; got != want { … }

// ❌ WRONG — wrong as soon as a column is dropped
total := 0
for _, col := range m.table.Table().Columns() { total += col.Width }
if want := width - 2 - len(cols)*2; total != want { … }
```

A column dropped for lack of room renders nothing — no header, no cell, no
padding — and its two cells go back into the budget. The sum of the declared
columns plus two each therefore asks for less than what the row occupies,
and fails on an otherwise correct layout. This is D61 seen from the other
side.

#### Which width library measures what

Lip Gloss v2 and the viewport measure with `x/ansi` (`ansi.StringWidth`,
grapheme clusters). `datatable` measures, truncates and pads by grapheme
clusters too (`ansi.FirstGraphemeCluster` with `ansi.GraphemeWidth`, the
primitive `StringWidth` sums; render.go, DEVDESK-280), so a cell is as wide for
the table as for Lip Gloss and the viewport, VS16 emoji and keycaps included.
`TestThemeStringWidthAgreesWithTheGraphemeWidth` (`internal/ui/theme/text_test.go`) pins the agreement for flags, ZWJ
sequences, Nerd Font glyphs, CJK and combining marks,
`TestDatatableMeasuresVS16LikeAnsi` for VS16 emoji (`❤️`, `✔️`), and
`TestDatatableMeasuresWithOneLibrary` for the whole table.
`runewidth.FillRight` remains for the indicator cell only (ambiguous-width
glyphs follow the terminal). The `theme.*` width helpers still measure with
`runewidth`, so they still count a VS16 emoji as 1 cell: do not size a table
with them. Whether the terminal draws a VS16 emoji in 1 or 2 cells depends on
mode 2027: Bubble Tea's renderer measures with WcWidth until the terminal
answers that mode (manual check, D117).

#### Every column declares its nature (§3.45)

`Sizing` has **no** default value: `SizingFixed` (exact width) or
`SizingContent` (content width, floored at `MinWidth`, capped at
`MaxWidth`). `TestEveryColumnDeclaresItsSizing` scans the sources and fails,
naming the file, line, and column.

`MinWidth` is a **floor**, not a request. What gives way beyond that is an
**entire** column: `Optional` ones first, rightmost first, then the others
if needed. The exception is an `Optional` column marked `YieldsToContent`: it
is removed, in drop order, before a required content column is cut below its
widest value (the order does not change, only the moment; DEVDESK-128). Fewer
correct columns beat all of them being wrong — truncating a
count column would render `142` as `14…`, and nothing on screen tells the
two apart.

Forbidden:
- ❌ Computing column widths inside a view
- ❌ Subtracting the borders before `Resize`, or clamping the width passed in
- ❌ Checking Rule 116 by summing the declared columns
- ❌ Leaving a column without a `Sizing`
- ❌ `Background()` on `s.Cell` (masks `s.Selected.Background()`)

### Rule 122 : `Cell` measures, `Style` colors — never the reverse ⚠️

**`Cell` returns plain text, with no ANSI sequence. Color goes through
`Style`, and through nothing else.**

**Why.** A cell is measured and truncated *before* it is dressed up, and the
measurement, which walks grapheme clusters, counts an escape sequence's
bytes as width (`bubbles/table` measured with `runewidth`, which does the same). A string of 7 visible cells carrying a color measures 28: it
therefore gets truncated in a column that is twice wide enough, and the cut
falls *inside* the escape sequence — `"\x1b[38;2;166;2…"`. The unterminated
sequence then bleeds onto every following row.

This is a limitation of `bubbles/table`, not of Bubble Tea or lipgloss, and
it is the same in Bubbles v2 (`charm.land/bubbles/v2`). `internal/ui/datatable` therefore
renders its own rows (`render.go`): the text is measured while still plain,
color is applied afterward. **The prohibition therefore targets `Cell`, not
color.**

```go
// ✅ CORRECT — the text is measurable, the color is decided separately
{
    Title: "Severity", MinWidth: 10,
    Cell:  func(f scan.Finding) string { return string(f.Severity) },
    Style: func(f scan.Finding) lipgloss.Style {
        return theme.SeverityTextStyle(string(f.Severity))
    },
}

// ❌ WRONG — color becomes part of what gets measured
{
    Cell: func(f scan.Finding) string {
        return theme.SeverityTextStyle(string(f.Severity)).Render(string(f.Severity))
    },
}
```

#### Two colors in one cell — `Cut` and `TailStyle`

**A cell can have two runs instead of one, and the measure-first order still
holds.** `Column.Cut(item) int` and `Column.TailStyle(item) lipgloss.Style`
exist for two callers — the containers load gauges (§3.71) and the `ws` Git
Status cell, whose branch keeps the text color while its markers warn
(§3.94) — so `Style` colors the first `Cut(item)` cells of the text and
`TailStyle` colors the rest. Every character either caller puts in such a cell
is single-width: `Cut` is a rune index, and a double-width glyph would move the
boundary. This is not the gradient the top of this rule forbids: `Cut` reads the
*already-fitted* plain text, after truncation and padding, at the exact point
`Style` already colors from — nothing styled is ever measured, it is the same
order applied to two runs. Nil on both (every column but the two gauges and
Git Status) keeps the one-run path.

```go
// ✅ CORRECT — two colors, both decided after Cell's text is final
{
    Title: "1 core", Sizing: SizingFixed, MinWidth: theme.GaugeWidth,
    Cell:      func(c docker.Container) string { return theme.Gauge(theme.GaugeWidth) },
    Style:     func(c docker.Container) lipgloss.Style { return theme.LoadTextStyle(c.CPUPercent) },
    Cut:       func(c docker.Container) int { return theme.GaugeFillWidth(c.CPUPercent, theme.GaugeWidth) },
    TailStyle: func(c docker.Container) lipgloss.Style { return theme.GaugeTrackStyle() },
}
```

Dropped only on a row a view has coloured whole (below) — error, busy, a CVE
severity — for the same reason `Style` is: a color that ends before the row
does would still close that solid highlight mid-row. On the plain "normal"
selection both runs *are* consulted, the same as `Style` is there.

#### N colored runs — `Spans`

`Column.Spans(item) []Span` generalises the two-run split to any number of
runs: `Span{Width, Style}` paints `Width` cells of the *finished* text, left to
right, and the cells left after the last span take `Style`. Same order as
`Cut`: the text is measured, truncated and padded first, then colored. A
negative width counts as 0, a zero width renders nothing (no empty ANSI
sequence), a span past the end of the cell is cut. Widths are rune counts, so
the cell holds single-width glyphs. A nil or empty result takes the ordinary
one-run path, byte for byte. **`Spans` takes precedence over `Cut`/`TailStyle`,
and a column declaring both is rejected** (`TestNoColumnDeclaresSpansWithCutOrTailStyle`).
Like `Cut`, spans are dropped on a row a view has coloured whole (error, busy,
severity) and repainted on `ColorTableLineSelected` and bold on the plain
"normal" selection.

#### Selected row

**`Style` is not consulted for a row a view has coloured whole** — error,
busy, a CVE severity, via `SelectedStyles` or the busy override. It is
handed to `styles.Selected` instead, and a color inside it closes with a
reset that carries away that solid background for the rest of the row: the
highlight would stop halfway through. That row answers "what state is this
in," and no column color is worth losing it.

**The plain "normal" selection is the exception (§3.72).**
`Style` *is* consulted there — `cellStyle` composites it with
`ColorTableLineSelected` and bold **on every cell itself**, rather than
dropping it for one outer wrap. That sidesteps the defect above instead of
reproducing it: a cell's own reset only ever uncovers the *same* background
the next cell immediately repaints, so nothing but that background is ever
exposed between two cells. `Cut`/`TailStyle` follow the same rule: both runs
repaint `ColorTableLineSelected` and bold themselves (`runStyle`'s
`selected` branch), so a reset between the two runs never uncovers anything
but that shared background either — a load gauge keeps its fill/track split
under the cursor instead of collapsing to `Style`'s single fill colour. The
track becomes a visible rail rather than an invisible one: its own colour
(`ColorSeverityLow`) and the selection background (`ColorTableLineSelected`)
are two distinct keys, not one aliased to the other.

#### Background

lipgloss does not inherit a background (Rule 115), and the viewport's style
only covers cells that emit nothing. `render.go` therefore gives an explicit
background to **every** cell of an unselected row, colored or not —
otherwise a single colored cell would strip the background off everything
that follows it. A column that declares only a `Foreground` automatically
receives `ColorBackground`.

#### Color discipline

A color that appears everywhere tells you nothing:

- a counter at `0`, a `-`, a missing value → `theme.DimStyle`;
- the nominal, majority state (a `running` container) → the default text
  color, **not** green;
- color is reserved for what deserves to be spotted without reading.

**The exception, and what defines it: a column where the absence of color
is already taken.** The `CI` column has three absences — never scanned, not
gradable, score withheld — and all three render in `DimStyle`. An `A` in
ordinary text color is distinguishable from a grey `-` only by a shade,
across four cells. Green there separates **a grade from an absence**, not
two nominal values from each other: that is exactly what the rule above
forbids elsewhere, and exactly what it requires here. That is the
criterion, and not "it's important" — if a column's absences were already
distinguishable, green would go back to being noise.

**The second and third declared exceptions: the containers load gauges
(§3.71).** Every cell of a gauge is the *same* glyph (`░`) — filled and empty
alike — so unlike every other colored column in this application, color here
is not a spotlight on top of text that already says something. It is the
**only** thing that says anything at all: with one glyph, a cell reads as
filled or empty exclusively by which color it carries.

- The *fill* is green below 75%, orange, then red, on Rule 128's ground:
  one alphabet of severity across the application, so a nearly-full gauge
  reads like a CRITICAL finding without reading the number beside it.
- The *track* — `theme.GaugeTrackStyle()`, aliasing `ColorSeverityLow` — is
  fixed, whatever the fill's own level is. Without it, an idle row's `░` and
  a critical row's `░` would carry whatever color `Style` had picked for
  that row's *fill*, which would read as the level bleeding into cells that
  were never filled. `ColorSeverityLow` defaults to the same tone as
  `ColorDim` (the counter zeroes above): the rail reads as unremarkable for
  the same reason a `0` does, which is the argument this bullet already
  makes generalised to a bar instead of a digit.

This is close to the CI column's own criterion (an idle gauge, entirely
track-colored, *is* what "no load" looks like) but reaches further: the CI
column's colors sit on top of letters that already read on their own; a
gauge's don't. Removing the color here does not fall back to plain text
that still says something — it falls back to a row of identical `░`.
Accepted cost, stated rather than discovered: most containers idle near zero,
so most rows carry a short green sliver in a track-colored field, both present
at once (`Cut`/`TailStyle`, above).

**The fourth declared exception: the Sig column's proven signature (§3.82).**
`internal/ui/sigcol` renders a Verified image's `IconOK` in green, while the
Update column (`theme.UpdateStyle`) renders its "up to date" `IconOK` dim. The
same glyph, two colors — and the reason is **not** the CI column's: in both
columns the glyphs already tell every state apart, so the shade is not what
separates the check mark from the `-`. The criterion is what the state *is*:

| | Update — "up to date" | Sig — Verified |
|---|---|---|
| How common | the majority, the resting state | rare: only images a rule covers, and only once proven |
| What it says | nothing happened, nothing to do | a guarantee was established for this digest |
| Its counterpart | a blue "update available" — the action | a red cross — the refusal |

Up to date is the nominal state this rule keeps out of color, exactly like a
`running` container. Verified is the positive half of a security verdict whose
negative half is red: dimming it would leave the column able to say only that
something is wrong, never that something was proven. That is the test for a
further exception of this kind, and not "it is good news": **a rare, established guarantee
whose absence or failure is itself colored**. A state that is merely the
common, fine case stays dim.

**The fifth declared exception: the token breakdown bars (DEVDESK-98).** A
`Spans` cell made of one repeated glyph, where color is the only way to tell
the parts of the bar apart. The criterion, and not "a bar looks nicer": the
cell repeats a single glyph so color is the only separator between its parts,
**and** the exact figures are readable without color on the same screen or one
key away (the numeric columns, the breakdown view). The colors name
**categories** (`theme.TokenStyle` roles: input, output, cache read, cache
write), never severity or gauge colors: a red part of a bar must not read as
"critical", nor a green one as "healthy". A bar whose figures are available
nowhere without color does not qualify. Accepted cost, stated rather than
discovered: without color the bar only says "has tokens"; the exact figures stay
readable elsewhere.

Checklist:
- [ ] No `style.Render(...)` inside what `Cell` returns
- [ ] Status icons as plain text: `theme.IconError + " error"`
- [ ] Per-cell color via `Style`, never via `Cell`
- [ ] Multi-run cells via Cut/TailStyle or Spans, never by styling inside Cell
- [ ] Selected-row color via `SelectedStyles` / `TableStylesForState/Severity()`
- [ ] Zeros and placeholders are `DimStyle`, not colored

### Rule 125 : Icon column alignment

> A row-level state (running, queued, failed, ...) is the activity column
> below, and `internal/app/activity_guard_test.go` enforces it (A-16,
> DEVDESK-143).

**Any icon column (or icon + short text) must be left-aligned.**

Nerd Font icons have variable width depending on the terminal. Left alignment is the only one that guarantees consistent rendering.

| Content type | Alignment |
|-----------------|------------|
| Icon alone | **Left** |
| Icon + short text | **Left** |
| Alphanumeric text | Left (default) |

#### An icon in the first column **is** a column

When a `datatable`'s first column carries a glyph, it is a column in its own
right — not a prefix stuck onto the neighboring text cell.

| | |
|---|---|
| Title | **empty**. The glyph reads in a glance; a header would be naming something that does not need naming, and `eza` does not put one there either. |
| Width | `datatable.IconColumnWidth` (2): the glyph, plus one cell so it does not touch the text. Two, not one — a Nerd Font glyph renders double-width on some terminals, and a single cell would truncate it there. |
| `Sizing` | `SizingFixed`. Nothing to measure. |
| `Less` / `Search` | **none**. It adds no text anyone could type, so filtering stays on the name columns; and a comparator would cost two more cells to fit its sort arrow. |

```go
// ✅ CORRECT — the glyph has its own column
{
    Title: "", Sizing: datatable.SizingFixed, MinWidth: datatable.IconColumnWidth,
    Cell: func(r row) string { return r.icon() },
},
{
    Title: "Name", Sizing: datatable.SizingContent, MinWidth: 16,
    Cell:   func(r row) string { return r.Name },
    Search: func(r row) string { return r.Name },
},

// ❌ WRONG — the glyph stuck into the identifying column
{
    Title: "Name", Sizing: datatable.SizingContent, MinWidth: 18,
    Cell: func(r row) string { return theme.IconDocker + " " + r.Name },
},
```

**What sticking it in costs**, and this is what settles it: the identifying
column spends its width on something that is not the name, and a
`SizingContent` then measures the glyph along with it — so the table's most
contested column reserves two cells for an icon, at every width.

#### An icon's color goes through a **role**, never through the glyph

Rule 122 applies here as everywhere: `Cell` renders the bare glyph, `Style`
colors it. What Rule 125 adds is **where the color comes from** —
`theme.IconStyle(role)`, and a role declared in `theme/iconcolors.go`.

```go
// ✅ CORRECT — the view names a meaning, the theme answers with a color
Cell:  func(r row) string { return nodeKindIcon(r.node) },
Style: func(r row) lipgloss.Style { return theme.IconStyle(nodeKindRole(r.node)) },

// ❌ WRONG — the view decides the hue
Style: func(r row) lipgloss.Style {
    return lipgloss.NewStyle().Foreground(theme.ColorSecondary)
},
```

**A codepoint is not a name.** A table of `U+F0849 → ColorSecondary` cannot
be reviewed: nothing on the line says whether the entry is correct, so an
error there is indistinguishable from a deliberate choice. A role can be
discussed, which is why it is the key.

The roles are overridable via a theme file (`icon_namespace`,
`icon_repository`, `icon_vis_*`, `icon_image`, `icon_container`; `IconRoleContainer`
is the resting icon of a running container, `ColorText` by default) — unlike syntax colors, which are closed
aliases: an icon is the first thing seen on a row, so it is the part of the
palette a user is most likely to have an opinion about.

**All three icon tables declare a `Style`** — `ws`, `:sec`, and the
explorer — and a fourth that did not declare one would be the application's
only monochrome icon column. A missing role shows: the cell falls back to
`ColorText` (see `IconColor`), so an oversight renders ordinary text rather
than nothing.

**The same object keeps its color from one view to another.** A git repo is
`IconRoleRepository` in `ws`, in `:sec`, and in the explorer — the role is
shared, not duplicated. This is the property for which the key is a meaning
rather than a glyph: the three views do not even show the same glyph for it.

**The granularity is that of the action, not that of the type.** `ws`
colors in three classes — repo, directory, file — which are exactly the
three branches of `availability.go`, and **not** a shade per language the
way `eza` does: `.go` versus `.rs` changes no shortcut on the row, so the
color would say nothing. An icon column is colored by what the row lets you
do.

**The color disappears under the cursor**, like that of any colored column:
the selected row is rendered whole by `styles.Selected` (Rule 122). An icon
column therefore cannot be the *only* carrier of a piece of information —
which is why the explorer's kind stays readable another way (the glyph
outside selection, the position in the tree inside it).

The three tables concerned are `ws`, `containers`, and the `:sec` inventory,
and they declare the same constant. `TestAnIconColumnIsUntitledAndTwoCellsWide`
(`internal/ui/datatable`) scans the sources and rejects a titleless column
that invents its own width. It does not see the other half — a glyph stuck
into a text cell is indistinguishable from a name that starts with a
glyph — which stays a matter for review.

#### The activity column

**In a view with long-running operations (jobs, agents, containers), the first
column is the activity indicator.** It is built by `datatable.IndicatorColumn`,
never by a literal `Column` with an `Indicator` field set (`TestOnlyIndicatorColumnSetsIndicator`
rejects it). It keeps the icon-column shape above: untitled, `SizingFixed`,
`datatable.IconColumnWidth`. When the row is at rest (`indicator.Idle`) the
cell shows the row's own icon via its `theme.IconStyle` role, or an empty cell.

- **The color says the state, never the operation.** A scan, a clone and a
  `docker stop` that are running all look the same: `●` / `○`. What is being
  done is the footer's and the Jobs view's business.
- **No green for "done".** `Done` is `◉` in `ColorActivityNeutral`. Green stays
  reserved for the exceptions Rule 122 lists.
- **The colors are closed aliases**, assigned in `ApplyTheme`:
  `ColorActivityRunning`, `ColorActivityNeutral`, `ColorActivitySuspended`,
  `ColorActivityFailed`. They are not `icon_*` roles and no theme file gains a
  key: a theme that retuned them per state would break the one alphabet of
  states the application shares.
- **The glyph carries the meaning, the color repeats it.** Under the cursor
  the color is repainted on `ColorTableLineSelected` and the glyph still reads.
- **The blink phase is read at render.** The router's `jobs.FrameMsg` carries
  it; the view calls `m.table.SetBlinkPhase(msg.Blink)` and nothing is rebuilt.
  Without the call the phase is on: a running row shows a steady `●`. A view
  starts no timer of its own for a row (`app.motion: static` pins it on).
- **Guarded.** `internal/app/activity_guard_test.go` (A-16, DEVDESK-143) fails
  a view whose table is neither on the activity column nor declared exempt, and
  a migrated package that holds `AdvanceSpinner`, `StatusColumn:`, a `Frame`
  field or a glyph literal. Details in `docs/architecture/app-shell.md`.

Forbidden:
- ❌ A literal `Column{Indicator: …}` instead of `datatable.IndicatorColumn`
- ❌ A glyph literal (`"●"`, `"⊗"`) in a view: use `indicator.Glyph`
- ❌ A color chosen in the view for an activity state
- ❌ Green for a finished operation
- ❌ A color that depends on the type of operation

Forbidden:
- ❌ `.Align(lipgloss.Center)` on an icon column
- ❌ `.Align(lipgloss.Right)` on an icon column
- ❌ A title above a glyph column
- ❌ A local width (`colIconFixed`, `statusColumnWidth`, a literal `2`) instead of `datatable.IconColumnWidth`
- ❌ A glyph prefixed inside a text column's cell
- ❌ An icon color chosen in the view instead of a `theme.IconStyle` role
- ❌ A color table indexed by the glyph rather than by meaning
- ❌ An icon column with no `Style`, while the other three have one
- ❌ A role per file type where the row offers the same actions

### Rule 139 : A `datatable`'s body is never replaced — not by a loading screen, not by a message

**A `datatable` stays a table, whatever it contains.** Whether it is
loading its data, empty because nothing has run yet, or empty because a
filter no longer matches anything, the rendered body is always
`m.table.View()` — header included, no rows. `datatable.View()` already
does this on its own: a zero-element table renders its header and fills
the rest with the background (`internal/ui/datatable/render.go`). Nothing
in a view therefore needs to detect this case.

What a body would have said instead — loading, the row count, a verdict —
is **the footer's and header's business**, never the body's:

- loading is a `components.Status{Text: "...", Activity: true}` in the
  footer, the shared dot, for a view's own load and for work the router
  tracks (Rule 128). That mark is for the *table's data*
  loading; an operation on one row is the row's activity dot (Rule 125),
  never a loading body;
- the row count, or whatever stands in for it (a verdict, a total), is a
  field of `GetHeaderInfo` (`shortcut.HeaderInfo{Key: "Images", Value: "0"}`) —
  it, not the body, answers "what am I looking at."

**Why.** A body that substitutes itself for the table — with a loading screen or
with text — loses its header and its columns for as long as the condition
holds, then regains them: the layout jumps on every refresh, every
`ctrl+r`, every keystroke in the filter. The header and the footer, on the
other hand, have a fixed height (Rule 124): what they display changes
without ever moving the table.

```go
// ✅ CORRECT — the body is always the table; the footer and header speak
func (m Model) renderImagesView() string {
    return m.imageTable.View()
}

### Rule 136 : Filter Bar for Tables

**Every table view must use `components.FilterBar` for search and toggle filters. No ad-hoc filter implementations.**

#### Behaviour

| State | Bar visible | Description |
|-------|-------------|-------------|
| No filter | ❌ | Bar is completely hidden |
| Toggle filter active | ✅ | Bar shows dimmed placeholder + active token(s) |
| Search mode (after `/`) | ✅ | Bar shows focused text input + active token(s) |
| Search confirmed (query set) | ✅ | Bar shows dimmed placeholder + query token + toggle tokens |

#### Visual

The filter bar forms a **closed rectangle** that visually connects with the viewport's bottom border:

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────┐   ← viewport top border
│  table rows...                          │
├─────────────────────────────────────────┤   ← viewport last line, joined (= rectangle top)
│  / cursor...         [tcp]  ·  [LISTEN] │   ← content line with │ sides
└─────────────────────────────────────────┘   ← rectangle bottom border
```

Both lines use `theme.ColorViewportBorder` for `│`, `└`, `┘`, `─` characters.
The viewport's last line is `└───┘` when no bar is shown and becomes `├───┤`
when one is.

**The router detects the bar from the shape of the footer's first line
(`components.OpensWithBarFrame`); no view declares it.** A footer only starts
with a `│…│` line through `components.BarFrame`: a view that draws its own
`│…│` first line would make the router join the viewport to it, so never do.

#### Placement — Footer, not viewport

The filter bar is rendered in `RenderFooter()`, **not** in the viewport content.

- `GetFooterHeight()` returns `baseFooterHeight + filterBar.ExtraHeight()`
- `RenderFooter()` prepends `filterBar.View()` when `filterBar.IsVisible()`
- Table height formula does **not** subtract `filterBar.ExtraHeight()` — the app router handles that via `GetFooterHeight()`

#### Integration Pattern

```go
// In Model struct
filterBar components.FilterBar  // or components.NewFilterBarWithTokens(tokens)

// In GetFooterHeight()
func (m Model) GetFooterHeight() int {
    return 2 + m.filterBar.ExtraHeight() // base (empty line + info) + filter bar
}

// In RenderFooter()
func (m Model) RenderFooter(width int) string {
    var parts []string
    if m.filterBar.IsVisible() {
        parts = append(parts, m.filterBar.View())
    }
    parts = append(parts, theme.EmptyLineBg(width), infoLine)
    return strings.Join(parts, "\n")
}

// In resize() / WindowSizeMsg handler — NO ExtraHeight subtraction
tableHeight := m.height - overhead  // overhead = header row only, NOT filterBar.ExtraHeight()
m.table.SetHeight(tableHeight)

// In Update() / key handler — forward keys when in search mode
if m.filterBar.InEditMode() {
    m.filterBar, cmd = m.filterBar.Update(msg)
    m.applyFilters()
    return m, cmd
}
// "/" key activates search
case "/":
    return m, m.filterBar.ActivateSearch()

// In InEditMode() — propagate to app router
func (m Model) InEditMode() bool {
    return m.filterBar.InEditMode() || /* other edit states */
}

// In View() / renderNormalView() — table only, NO filter bar here
func (m Model) renderNormalView() string {
    return m.table.View()
}

// In applyFilters() — use filterBar.SearchQuery() for text filtering
query := strings.ToLower(m.filterBar.SearchQuery())
```

#### Toggle filter tokens (views with dedicated filter keys)

Use `components.NewFilterBarWithTokens()` and update token active state when toggle keys are pressed:

```go
// Init
fb := components.NewFilterBarWithTokens([]components.FilterToken{
    {Label: "tcp"},
    {Label: "udp"},
})

// On key "t"
fb.SetTokenActive("tcp", !fb.IsTokenActive("tcp"))
```

#### Rules

- ✅ Use `components.FilterBar` — never re-implement the filter bar locally
- ✅ The frame itself is `components.BarFrame(width, inner)`: that is what
  `FilterBar.View()` calls, and the only path for whatever shares this slot
  without being a filter — the viewer's go-to-line prompt (§3.53). Two
  implementations of the rectangle would be free to diverge on where the
  corners sit.
- ✅ Only one occupant of the slot at a time, and the height does not depend
  on which one — otherwise the panel resizes under the reader whenever one
  opens on top of the other.
- ✅ `filterBar.ExtraHeight()` must be added to `GetFooterHeight()` return value
- ✅ `filterBar.View()` must be prepended in `RenderFooter()` when `filterBar.IsVisible()`
- ✅ `filterBar.InEditMode()` must propagate via the view's `InEditMode()` method
- ✅ `"/"` key must always call `filterBar.ActivateSearch()`
- ❌ Filter bar must NOT be rendered inside the viewport (`View()` / `renderNormalView()`)
- ❌ `filterBar.ExtraHeight()` must NOT be subtracted from table height (app router handles it)
- ❌ `filterInput textinput.Model` fields in view models (use FilterBar instead)

## Code quality rules and proactive checks

### Rule 301 : Systematic code quality check before commit

**MANDATORY**: Before creating a commit, ALWAYS perform the following checks:

#### 1. Go linter (golangci-lint)
```bash
golangci-lint run
```

**Required actions:**
- ✅ Fix ALL warnings and errors
- ✅ Specifically check deprecation warnings (SA1019)
- ✅ NEVER ignore warnings without documented justification

#### 2. Tests
```bash
go test ./...
```

**Required actions:**
- ✅ Verify that all tests pass
- ✅ If tests fail, fix them BEFORE the commit

#### 3. Build
```bash
go build
```

**Required actions:**
- ✅ Verify that the build succeeds without errors
- ✅ Test the application if functional changes were made

#### 4. Deprecated dependencies

**Detection:**
- Check golangci-lint SA1019 warnings
- Look in go.mod for packages marked as deprecated

**Action:**
- Replace IMMEDIATELY with a maintained alternative
- Document the replacement in the commit message
- Update the documentation (.claude/CLAUDE.md)

**Examples of common replacements:**
- `github.com/go-ping/ping` → `github.com/prometheus-community/pro-bing`

### Rule 302 : IDE diagnostics check

**MANDATORY**: Before each commit, check the IDE diagnostics:

```
Use mcp__ide__getDiagnostics to check:
- Compilation errors
- Unused parameters
- Unused imports
- Other warnings
```

**Required actions:**
- ✅ Fix or justify every diagnostic
- ✅ Do not ignore "unused parameter" without a reason

### Rule 303 : go.mod and dependencies

**After any dependency change:**

```bash
go mod tidy
go mod verify
```

**Required actions:**
- ✅ Verify that go.mod is up to date
- ✅ Verify that go.sum is consistent
- ✅ Document new dependencies in .claude/CLAUDE.md

### Rule 304 : Quality commit message

**Mandatory format for quality fixes — in English (see Rule 307):**

```
type: short description

Detailed description explaining:
- What was detected (warning, error, etc.)
- Why it was a problem
- How it was resolved

Co-Authored-By: Claude Sonnet 4.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
```

**Commit types for quality:**
- `fix:` - Bug fix detected by linter
- `chore:` - Deprecated dependency replacement
- `refactor:` - Code quality improvement

### Rule 305 : MANDATORY pre-commit checklist

**Before EVERY commit, check:**

- [ ] `golangci-lint run` → 0 warnings
- [ ] `go test ./...` → PASS
- [ ] `go build` → SUCCESS
- [ ] `mcp__ide__getDiagnostics` → No critical error
- [ ] `go.mod` up to date (if dependencies changed)
- [ ] Documentation updated (if API changed)
- [ ] Tests added (if new feature)

**If EVEN ONE of these checks fails:**
- ❌ DO NOT create the commit
- ✅ Fix it first
- ✅ Restart the checklist

### Rule 306 : MANDATORY proactivity

**Claude Code MUST:**
- ✅ Check the linter WITHOUT the user asking
- ✅ Propose fixes BEFORE the commit
- ✅ Flag deprecated dependencies AS SOON AS they are detected
- ✅ Document all quality changes

**Claude Code MUST NEVER:**
- ❌ Wait for the user to flag a warning
- ❌ Create a commit with unresolved warnings
- ❌ Ignore dependency issues
- ❌ Forget to update the documentation

### Correct workflow examples

**Example 1 - Feature commit:**
```
1. Write the code
2. go build → verify compilation
3. golangci-lint run → fix warnings
4. go test ./... → verify tests
5. mcp__ide__getDiagnostics → check the IDE
6. git commit with a detailed message
```

**Example 2 - Detecting a deprecated dependency:**
```
1. golangci-lint detects SA1019
2. Look up the recommended alternative
3. Replace the import and the code
4. go mod tidy
5. Test that everything works
6. Update .claude/CLAUDE.md
7. git commit explaining the replacement
```

### Rule 307 : Commits and code comments — English only

**Every git commit message and every comment in the code must be written
in English**, regardless of the language used to converse with the user.

## Code editing instructions

### Rule 201 : Code must be clean, concise, and well-structured to stay maintainable

#### Extracting functions from Update()
- **Strict limit**: If a case in `Update(msg tea.Msg)` exceeds **5 lines**, extract it into a separate function
- **Naming**: `handle[MessageType]` (e.g. `handleContextSwitch()`, `handleKeyPress()`)
- **Pattern**: The function must return `(tea.Model, tea.Cmd)`

**Before (bad):**
```go
case ContextSwitchCompleteMsg:
    a.config = msg.Config
    a.currentContext = msg.ContextName
    a.reinitializeViews(msg.Config)
    return a, func() tea.Msg {
        return tea.WindowSizeMsg{Width: a.width, Height: a.height}
    }
```

**After (good):**
```go
case ContextSwitchCompleteMsg:
    return a.handleContextSwitch(msg)

// Further down in the file
func (a *App) handleContextSwitch(msg ContextSwitchCompleteMsg) (tea.Model, tea.Cmd) {
    a.config = msg.Config
    a.currentContext = msg.ContextName
    a.reinitializeViews(msg.Config)
    return a, func() tea.Msg {
        return tea.WindowSizeMsg{Width: a.width, Height: a.height}
    }
}
```

#### Code reuse
- **Zero duplication**: If a block of code appears 2+ times, create a function
- **Modules**: Group related functions together (e.g. all context switching in a single file)
- **Constants**: Extract magic values into named constants

#### Error handling
- **Bubble Tea pattern**: Errors = messages (e.g. `ContextSwitchErrorMsg`)
- **Always log** in DEBUG mode: `log.Printf("ERROR: %v", err)`
- **Never ignore**: If the error is non-critical, document why

#### Comments
- **Mandatory for**:
  - Exported (public) functions
  - Complex business logic
  - Workarounds or non-obvious decisions
- **Format**: `// functionName does X and returns Y`
- **Avoid**: Comments that repeat the code

#### Complexity
- **Maximum 3 levels of indentation** in a function
- **Functions > 50 lines**: refactor into smaller functions
- **Switch > 10 cases**: consider a table-driven pattern

235	// numbers on the tab labels, and scan.Result's counters are the same ones.
236	func (m *Model) countFindingsByTab() (cve, secrets, licenses, misconfigs, ci int) {
237		if m.result == nil {
238			return 0, 0, 0, 0, 0
239		}
240	
241		for _, f := range m.result.Findings {
242			switch scan.Categorize(f) {
243			case scan.CategoryVulnerability:
244				cve++
245			case scan.CategorySecret:
246				secrets++
247			case scan.CategoryLicense:
248				licenses++
249			case scan.CategoryMisconfiguration:
250				misconfigs++
251			case scan.CategoryCIScore:
252				ci++
253			}
254		}
255		return cve, secrets, licenses, misconfigs, ci
256	}

290	// handleIgnoreSecret prompts confirmation to ignore a secret finding.
291	//
292	// Gitleaks findings only. .gitleaksignore is matched on a Gitleaks fingerprint,
293	// which a Trivy secret does not have — AddToGitleaksIgnore would fabricate one
294	// from the file and rule, write it, and report success for a line Gitleaks will
295	// never match and Trivy never reads. Refusing says so instead.
296	func (m Model) handleIgnoreSecret() (tea.Model, tea.Cmd) {
297		if exclude := m.canExclude(); !exclude.Enabled() {
298			return m, m.footer.Warn(exclude.Reason)
299		}
300		finding, _ := m.subjectFinding()
301		m.findingToIgnore = &finding
302		m.confirmModal = sharedcomponents.NewConfirmModal(
303			"Ignore Secret",
304			fmt.Sprintf("Add this secret to .gitleaksignore?\n\nFile: %s\nRule: %s", finding.File, finding.ID),
305		)
306		return m, nil
307	}

309	// The two findings actions, and why each does not apply (Rule 130).
310	const (
311		reasonNoFinding    = "No finding selected"
312		reasonNotASecret   = "REDACTED"
313		reasonNotGitleaks  = "Only Gitleaks findings can be added to .gitleaksignore"
314		reasonNotCITab     = "The resolved pipeline belongs to the CI tab"
315		reasonNotARepo     = "An image has no pipeline"
316		reasonNoResolution = "This forge does not resolve a pipeline server-side"
317		reasonNothingToSee = "No finding to open"
318	)

320	// canOpenFinding reports whether enter has a row to detail.
321	func (m Model) canOpenFinding() shortcut.Availability {
322		if _, ok := m.findingsTable.Selected(); !ok {
323			return shortcut.Unavailable(reasonNothingToSee)
324		}
325		return shortcut.Availability{}

328	// canExclude reports whether X applies to the selected finding.
329	//
330	// .gitleaksignore is matched on a Gitleaks fingerprint, which a Trivy secret
331	// does not have — fabricating one would report success for a line nothing will
332	// ever match. The tab is checked first because it is the coarser answer: on
333	// the CVE tab the key means nothing at all, whatever the row.
334	// openPipelineKey opens the pipeline the forge resolves for this repository.
335	//
336	// It is a **declared exception** to the uppercase vocabulary
337	// (keymap.DeclaredExceptions), on the precedent of `c` in oci/network-inspect
338	// and for the reason written there: the action exists on one sub-screen, and
339	// burning one of the three remaining free capitals for it would cost more than
340	// it returns.
341	//
342	// `o` and not `p`: `o` already means "open what this screen points at" in this
343	// view's details state, where it opens a finding's reference. One verb, two
344	// screens, and the shortcut column is replaced by the mode either way.
345	const openPipelineKey = "o"
346	
347	// canOpenPipeline decides whether the resolved pipeline can be fetched.
348	//
349	// The tab is checked first for canExclude's reason — it is the coarser answer,
350	// and off the CI tab the key means nothing whatever the row. The shape is
351	// checked before anything is read: a GitHub context cannot answer this at all,
352	// and finding that out after a keystroke and a git call would be worse than
353	// saying so in the column.
354	func (m Model) canOpenPipeline() shortcut.Availability {
355		switch {
356		case m.activeTab != TabCIScore:
357			return shortcut.Unavailable(reasonNotCITab)
358		case m.result == nil || m.result.TargetType != scan.TargetDirectory:
359			return shortcut.Unavailable(reasonNotARepo)
360		case !forge.ShapeFor(m.config.Forge.Type).MergedCIConfig:
361			return shortcut.Unavailable(reasonNoResolution)
362		}
363		return shortcut.Availability{}
364	}

366	// openResolvedPipeline hands the document to the router, which opens the
367	// viewer on it. The fetch is the source's, so it runs on the viewer's own Cmd
368	// (Rule 110) and its failures are reported where the document would have been.
369	func (m Model) openResolvedPipeline() (tea.Model, tea.Cmd) {
370		// The refusal is never silent (Rule 130), and it is a Warn rather than an
371		// Error: nothing failed, the key does not apply as asked (Rule 128). The
372		// reason is the one canOpenPipeline computed, so the footer and the greyed
373		// entry cannot be about different things.
374		if a := m.canOpenPipeline(); !a.Enabled() {
375			return m, m.footer.Warn(a.Reason)
376		}
377		source := pipelineSource{
378			RepoPath: m.result.Target,
379			Label:    theme.FoldHome(m.result.Target),
380			Forge:    m.config.Forge,
381			Secrets:  m.secrets,
382			Findings: m.result.Findings,
383		}
384		return m, func() tea.Msg { return uiviewer.OpenRequestMsg{Source: source} }
385	}

387	func (m Model) canExclude() shortcut.Availability {
388		if m.activeTab != TabSecrets {
389			return shortcut.Unavailable(reasonNotASecret)
390		}
391		finding, ok := m.subjectFinding()
392		switch {
393		case !ok:
394			return shortcut.Unavailable(reasonNoFinding)
395		case finding.Source != scan.SourceGitleaks:
396			return shortcut.Unavailable(reasonNotGitleaks)
397		}
398		return shortcut.Availability{}
399	}

401	// handleResultsState processes input in results state.
402	//
403	// The search answers first, and every key below is unreachable while it has the
404	// keyboard: "c" is a character in a query, "esc" cancels the search rather than
405	// leaving the results, and "enter" confirms it rather than opening a finding.
406	// The inventory has had this guard since it gained a bar; this state gained one
407	// the day the severity floor became tokens, and never got the guard with it.
408	func (m Model) handleResultsState(msg tea.KeyPressMsg) (tea.Model, tea.Cmd) {
409		if m.findingsTable.InEditMode() {
410			return m, m.findingsTable.Update(msg)
411		}
412		if m.activeTab == TabRemediation {
413			if next, cmd, handled := m.handleRemediationKey(msg); handled {
414				return next, cmd
415			}
416		}
417		switch msg.String() {
418		case "esc":
419			// No origin view means this view was opened directly, so esc stays
420			// inside it and goes back to whichever landing state it opened on.
421			if m.OriginView == "" {
422				return m.goHome()
423			}
424			return m, func() tea.Msg { return BackToOriginMsg{Origin: m.OriginView} }
425		case "enter":
426			var preview tea.Cmd
427			if finding, ok := m.findingsTable.Selected(); ok {
428				// The details view is about a finding, not about a row index — an
429				// index would name a different one the moment the list changed
430				// under it, which is how workspaces got D24.
431				m.selectedFinding = &finding
432				m.state = StateDetails
433				m.sizeDetails()
434				preview = m.startChangePreview()
435				m.detailsViewport.SetContent(m.buildDetailsContent())
436				m.detailsViewport.GotoTop()
437			}
438			return m, preview
439		case "ctrl+r":
440			m.activeTab = TabCVE
441			return m.goHome()
442		case "tab":
443			m.switchTab((m.activeTab + 1) % tabCount)
444			cmd := m.enterTab()
445			return m, cmd
446		case "shift+tab":
447			m.switchTab((m.activeTab + tabCount - 1) % tabCount)
448			cmd := m.enterTab()
449			return m, cmd
450		// 1-4 jumped straight to a tab. They were the application's only numeric
451		// bindings, and an exception in a single view is precisely what §3.26
452		// dismantles — tab reaches all four.
453		case "c", "h", "m", "l":
454			return m.toggleSeverity(msg.String())
455		case pssFilterKey:
456			return m.togglePSS()
457		case keymap.Exclude:
458			return m.handleIgnoreSecret()
459		case openPipelineKey:
460			return m.openResolvedPipeline()
461		case keymap.Scan:
462			// Off the Remediation tab this refuses, with the reason (Rule 130).
463			return m.scanCandidates()
464		case writeRemediationKey:
465			// One key, one verb — write the file — applied to whichever tab's
466			// object. The Remediation tab writes a base image, the
467			// Misconfigurations tab a built-in fix; anywhere else the refusal says
468			// which tab it belongs to (Rule 130).
469			if m.activeTab == TabMisconfig {
470				return m.prepareMisconfigFix()
471			}
472			return m.prepareRemediationWrite()
473		}
474		// `.` is the sort again, and the search and the severity tokens are the
475		// table's (Rule 136).
476		return m, m.findingsTable.Update(msg)
477	}
478	
479	// toggleSeverity flips one severity token. Cumulative: c and h together ask for
480	// "CRITICAL or HIGH", which is the question a threshold cycle could not put.
481	func (m Model) toggleSeverity(key string) (tea.Model, tea.Cmd) {
482		label := map[string]string{"c": "critical", "h": "high", "m": "medium", "l": "low"}[key]
483		m.findingsTable.SetTokenActive(label, !m.findingsTable.IsTokenActive(label))
484		m.findingsTable.GotoTop()
485		return m, nil
486	}

488	// resizeFindings lays the findings table out. Every tab gets the whole height:
489	// the CI tab used to give two rows to a score line above the table, and losing
490	// two findings on one tab out of five — for a letter the inventory already
491	// carries per target — was not worth the jump on every tab switch.
492	func (m *Model) resizeFindings() {
493		// The File column belongs to the Misconfigurations tab: the same rule
494		// there can fire in many files, and nowhere else it says nothing more than
495		// the title. Done here, with the size, so a tab switch and a resize cannot
496		// disagree.
497		m.findingsTable.SetColumnHidden(fileColumn, m.activeTab != TabMisconfig)
498		m.findingsTable.Resize(m.width, max(m.height, 5))
499		m.remediation.table.Resize(m.width, max(m.height, 5))
500	}

20	// findingColumns describes the findings table.
21	//
22	// The table opens on the order the scanner reported — `SortColumn: -1`, which
23	// datatable keeps as a stop on the cycle, so `.` always leads back to it. Every
24	// column sorts, because `.` was handed back to the sort when the severity floor
25	// became four tokens (§3.26) and then no column was ever given a `Less`:
26	// CycleSort returned on its first line and the header advertised a key that did
27	// nothing at all.
28	//
29	// Three columns search, and that is not optional either. Declaring tokens makes
30	// `Searchable()` true, so `/` already opened a query — against no searchable
31	// column, which matches nothing and empties the table. The bar's own left half
32	// says `/ search...` whether or not anything answers it.
33	//
34	// Severity searches nothing on purpose: c/h/m/l are the severity filter, and a
35	// second way to ask one question is what this codebase spends its time
36	// removing. The Title is not pre-truncated either — bubbles cuts every cell to
37	// its column width with the same ellipsis, and doing it by hand at width-3
38	// first only cost three characters of title.
39	func findingColumns() []datatable.Column[scan.Finding] {
40		return []datatable.Column[scan.Finding]{
41			{
42				Title: "Severity", Sizing: datatable.SizingFixed, MinWidth: 10,
43				Cell: func(f scan.Finding) string { return string(f.Severity) },
44				// The same palette the selected row uses, so a severity reads the
45				// same colour whether or not the cursor is on it.
46				Style: func(f scan.Finding) lipgloss.Style { return theme.SeverityTextStyle(string(f.Severity)) },
47				Less:  func(a, b scan.Finding) bool { return severityRank(a.Severity) < severityRank(b.Severity) },
48			},
49			{
50				Title: "ID", Sizing: datatable.SizingContent, MinWidth: 18,
51				Cell:   func(f scan.Finding) string { return f.ID },
52				Less:   func(a, b scan.Finding) bool { return a.ID < b.ID },
53				Search: func(f scan.Finding) string { return f.ID },
54			},
55			{
56				Title: "Title", Sizing: datatable.SizingContent, MinWidth: 20, Flex: 1,
57				// The Pod Security label is a prefix of the text (DEVDESK-686); the
58				// sort stays on the title and the search sees the label.
59				Cell:   titleWithLabel,
60				Less:   func(a, b scan.Finding) bool { return a.Title < b.Title },
61				Search: func(f scan.Finding) string { return titleWithLabel(f) + " " + f.PkgName + " " + f.File },
62			},
63			{
64				Title: "Source", Sizing: datatable.SizingFixed, Optional: true, MinWidth: 14,
65				Cell:   sourceDisplay,
66				Less:   func(a, b scan.Finding) bool { return sourceDisplay(a) < sourceDisplay(b) },
67				Search: sourceDisplay,
68			},
69			{
70				// Appended last, so the indices above do not move. No Less and no
71				// Search: the Title search already matches the file, and a second
72				// way to ask the same question is noise. It keeps the end of a long
73				// path, which is what tells two findings apart.
74				Title: "File", Sizing: datatable.SizingContent, MinWidth: 16, MaxWidth: 40,
75				Optional: true, TruncateHead: true,
76				Cell: fileCell,
77			},
78		}
79	}
80	
81	// fileColumn is the index of the File column in findingColumns.
82	const fileColumn = 4
83	
84	// fileCell is the File cell: plain text (Rule 122), with the scanner container's
85	// mount removed and a path under HOME folded. The columns are built once, before
86	// any result exists, so the cell does not know the scanned target (the detail
87	// does): an absolute path under the target shows as the folded absolute path here
88	// and as a relative one in the detail. Trivy reports relative paths, so this is
89	// the rare case.
90	func fileCell(f scan.Finding) string { return shortPaths(f.File, "") }
91	
92	// severityRank orders the levels by how bad they are, which is the only order
93	// worth sorting this column by: alphabetically, CRITICAL lands between no two
94	// levels it belongs with — HIGH, LOW, MEDIUM — so a descending sort would put
95	// MEDIUM at the top and bury the finding the user opened the view for.
96	//
97	// Ascending is least-severe-first, so `.`'s second press (descending, Rule 111)
98	// is the one that answers "what is worst here".
99	//
100	// UNKNOWN ranks below LOW rather than above CRITICAL: it is what a scanner
101	// says when it has no score, not a claim that something is worse than critical.
102	// It has no token either, for the same reason — see severityToken.
103	func severityRank(s scan.SeverityLevel) int {
104		switch s {
105		case scan.SeverityCritical:
106			return 4
107		case scan.SeverityHigh:
108			return 3
109		case scan.SeverityMedium:
110			return 2
111		case scan.SeverityLow:
112			return 1
113		default:
114			return 0
115		}
116	}

137	// updateFindingsTable populates the findings table based on active tab and filters.
138	//
139	// The tab is this view's own filter, not the component's: it selects which
140	// findings exist at all, where a FilterBar query narrows a list that is already
141	// settled. The severity went the other way — it is four cumulative tokens the
142	// table owns (Rule 136), which is what gave `.` back to the sort.
143	func (m *Model) updateFindingsTable() {
144		if m.result == nil {
145			return
146		}
147	
148		m.findingsTable.SetItems(m.filterFindingsByTab())
149		// A change of tab or severity is a change of scope, not a shorter list, so
150		// the cursor goes back to the top and the columns are measured again.
151		// SetItems deliberately does neither on its own.
152		m.findingsTable.GotoTop()
153		m.findingsTable.Remeasure()
154	}

156	// tabCategory maps a tab to the finding category it shows.
157	//
158	// The tabs and scan.Result's counters are now the same classification, applied
159	// once in scan.Categorize: they were two rules that disagreed on three inputs,
160	// each of which produced a finding counted in the header but present in no tab
161	// at all — visible nowhere, which is the worst way for a finding to be wrong.
162	var tabCategory = map[int]scan.Category{
163		TabCVE:       scan.CategoryVulnerability,
164		TabSecrets:   scan.CategorySecret,
165		TabLicense:   scan.CategoryLicense,
166		TabMisconfig: scan.CategoryMisconfiguration,
167		TabCIScore:   scan.CategoryCIScore,

170	// filterFindingsByTab returns findings filtered by the active tab
171	func (m *Model) filterFindingsByTab() []scan.Finding {
172		if m.result == nil {
173			return nil
174		}
175	
176		want, ok := tabCategory[m.activeTab]
177		if !ok {
178			return nil
179		}
180		var filtered []scan.Finding
181		for _, f := range m.result.Findings {
182			if scan.Categorize(f) == want {
183				filtered = append(filtered, f)
184			}
185		}
186		return filtered
187	}

189	// sourceDisplay returns a display string for the source column.
190	//
191	// Which tool found it, not which category it is — the tab already says the
192	// category, and telling gitleaks from trivy-secret in the Secrets tab is the
193	// point of showing both there.
194	//
195	// A Trivy misconfiguration shows its dialect instead (§3.80): "misconfig"
196	// only repeated the tab's name, while "kubernetes", "helm" or "dockerfile"
197	// is what tells a Deployment's rule from a Dockerfile's on a tab that lists
198	// both — and it is searchable, so `/helm` narrows to the charts. A column of
199	// its own was the alternative, but every other tab would have carried it
200	// empty. A result cached before the dialect was recorded keeps "misconfig".
201	func sourceDisplay(f scan.Finding) string {
202		switch f.Source {
203		case scan.SourceTrivyLicense:
204			return "license"
205		case scan.SourceTrivyMisconfig:
206			if f.IaCType != "" {
207				return f.IaCType
208			}
209			return "misconfig"
210		case scan.SourceKubeconform:
211			// Schema validation, which is what separates it from Trivy's
212			// kubernetes findings on the same manifest.
213			return "schema"
214		case scan.SourceHelm:
215			// Not "helm": that is already the dialect of Trivy's chart findings.
216			return "helm lint"
217		case scan.SourceKustomize:
218			return "kustomize"
219		case scan.SourceBuildContext:
220			// DevDesk's own check (§3.81): what a COPY of the whole context takes
221			// into the image, which no scanner reports.
222			return "context"
223		case scan.SourceGitleaks:
224			return "gitleaks"
225		case scan.SourceTrivySecret:
226			return "trivy"
227		case scan.SourceTrivy:
228			return "vuln"
229		default:
230			return f.Source
231		}
232	}

235	// numbers on the tab labels, and scan.Result's counters are the same ones.
236	func (m *Model) countFindingsByTab() (cve, secrets, licenses, misconfigs, ci int) {
237		if m.result == nil {
238			return 0, 0, 0, 0, 0
239		}

241		for _, f := range m.result.Findings {
242			switch scan.Categorize(f) {
243			case scan.CategoryVulnerability:
244				cve++
245			case scan.CategorySecret:
246				secrets++
247			case scan.CategoryLicense:

250				misconfigs++
251			case scan.CategoryCIScore:
252				ci++
253			}
254		}
255		return cve, secrets, licenses, misconfigs, ci
256	}

290	// handleIgnoreSecret prompts confirmation to ignore a secret finding.
291	//
292	// Gitleaks findings only. .gitleaksignore is matched on a Gitleaks fingerprint,
293	// which a Trivy secret does not have — AddToGitleaksIgnore would fabricate one
294	// from the file and rule, write it, and report success for a line Gitleaks will
295	// never match and Trivy never reads. Refusing says so instead.
296	func (m Model) handleIgnoreSecret() (tea.Model, tea.Cmd) {
297		if exclude := m.canExclude(); !exclude.Enabled() {
298			return m, m.footer.Warn(exclude.Reason)
299		}
300		finding, _ := m.subjectFinding()
301		m.findingToIgnore = &finding
302		m.confirmModal = sharedcomponents.NewConfirmModal(
303			"Ignore Secret",
304			fmt.Sprintf("Add this secret to .gitleaksignore?\n\nFile: %s\nRule: %s", finding.File, finding.ID),
305		)
306		return m, nil
307	}
308	
309	// The two findings actions, and why each does not apply (Rule 130).
310	const (
311		reasonNoFinding    = "No finding selected"
312		reasonNotASecret   = "REDACTED"
313		reasonNotGitleaks  = "Only Gitleaks findings can be added to .gitleaksignore"
314		reasonNotCITab     = "The resolved pipeline belongs to the CI tab"
315		reasonNotARepo     = "An image has no pipeline"
316		reasonNoResolution = "This forge does not resolve a pipeline server-side"
317		reasonNothingToSee = "No finding to open"
318	)
319	
320	// canOpenFinding reports whether enter has a row to detail.
321	func (m Model) canOpenFinding() shortcut.Availability {
322		if _, ok := m.findingsTable.Selected(); !ok {
323			return shortcut.Unavailable(reasonNothingToSee)
324		}
325		return shortcut.Availability{}
326	}
327	
328	// canExclude reports whether X applies to the selected finding.
329	//
330	// .gitleaksignore is matched on a Gitleaks fingerprint, which a Trivy secret
331	// does not have — fabricating one would report success for a line nothing will
332	// ever match. The tab is checked first because it is the coarser answer: on
333	// the CVE tab the key means nothing at all, whatever the row.
334	// openPipelineKey opens the pipeline the forge resolves for this repository.
335	//
336	// It is a **declared exception** to the uppercase vocabulary
337	// (keymap.DeclaredExceptions), on the precedent of `c` in oci/network-inspect
338	// and for the reason written there: the action exists on one sub-screen, and
339	// burning one of the three remaining free capitals for it would cost more than
340	// it returns.
341	//
342	// `o` and not `p`: `o` already means "open what this screen points at" in this
343	// view's details state, where it opens a finding's reference. One verb, two
344	// screens, and the shortcut column is replaced by the mode either way.
345	const openPipelineKey = "o"
346	
347	// canOpenPipeline decides whether the resolved pipeline can be fetched.
348	//
349	// The tab is checked first for canExclude's reason — it is the coarser answer,
350	// and off the CI tab the key means nothing whatever the row. The shape is
351	// checked before anything is read: a GitHub context cannot answer this at all,
352	// and finding that out after a keystroke and a git call would be worse than
353	// saying so in the column.
354	func (m Model) canOpenPipeline() shortcut.Availability {
355		switch {
356		case m.activeTab != TabCIScore:
357			return shortcut.Unavailable(reasonNotCITab)
358		case m.result == nil || m.result.TargetType != scan.TargetDirectory:
359			return shortcut.Unavailable(reasonNotARepo)
360		case !forge.ShapeFor(m.config.Forge.Type).MergedCIConfig:
361			return shortcut.Unavailable(reasonNoResolution)
362		}
363		return shortcut.Availability{}
364	}
365	
366	// openResolvedPipeline hands the document to the router, which opens the
367	// viewer on it. The fetch is the source's, so it runs on the viewer's own Cmd
368	// (Rule 110) and its failures are reported where the document would have been.
369	func (m Model) openResolvedPipeline() (tea.Model, tea.Cmd) {
370		// The refusal is never silent (Rule 130), and it is a Warn rather than an
371		// Error: nothing failed, the key does not apply as asked (Rule 128). The
372		// reason is the one canOpenPipeline computed, so the footer and the greyed
373		// entry cannot be about different things.
374		if a := m.canOpenPipeline(); !a.Enabled() {
375			return m, m.footer.Warn(a.Reason)
376		}
377		source := pipelineSource{
378			RepoPath: m.result.Target,
379			Label:    theme.FoldHome(m.result.Target),
380			Forge:    m.config.Forge,
381			Secrets:  m.secrets,
382			Findings: m.result.Findings,
383		}
384		return m, func() tea.Msg { return uiviewer.OpenRequestMsg{Source: source} }
385	}
386	
387	func (m Model) canExclude() shortcut.Availability {
388		if m.activeTab != TabSecrets {
389			return shortcut.Unavailable(reasonNotASecret)
390		}
391		finding, ok := m.subjectFinding()
392		switch {
393		case !ok:
394			return shortcut.Unavailable(reasonNoFinding)
395		case finding.Source != scan.SourceGitleaks:
396			return shortcut.Unavailable(reasonNotGitleaks)
397		}
398		return shortcut.Availability{}
399	}
400	
401	// handleResultsState processes input in results state.
402	//
403	// The search answers first, and every key below is unreachable while it has the
404	// keyboard: "c" is a character in a query, "esc" cancels the search rather than
405	// leaving the results, and "enter" confirms it rather than opening a finding.
406	// The inventory has had this guard since it gained a bar; this state gained one
407	// the day the severity floor became tokens, and never got the guard with it.
408	func (m Model) handleResultsState(msg tea.KeyPressMsg) (tea.Model, tea.Cmd) {
409		if m.findingsTable.InEditMode() {
410			return m, m.findingsTable.Update(msg)
411		}
412		if m.activeTab == TabRemediation {
413			if next, cmd, handled := m.handleRemediationKey(msg); handled {
414				return next, cmd
415			}
416		}
417		switch msg.String() {
418		case "esc":
419			// No origin view means this view was opened directly, so esc stays
420			// inside it and goes back to whichever landing state it opened on.
421			if m.OriginView == "" {
422				return m.goHome()
423			}
424			return m, func() tea.Msg { return BackToOriginMsg{Origin: m.OriginView} }
425		case "enter":
426			var preview tea.Cmd
427			if finding, ok := m.findingsTable.Selected(); ok {
428				// The details view is about a finding, not about a row index — an
429				// index would name a different one the moment the list changed
430				// under it, which is how workspaces got D24.
431				m.selectedFinding = &finding
432				m.state = StateDetails
433				m.sizeDetails()
434				preview = m.startChangePreview()
435				m.detailsViewport.SetContent(m.buildDetailsContent())
436				m.detailsViewport.GotoTop()
437			}
438			return m, preview
439		case "ctrl+r":
440			m.activeTab = TabCVE
441			return m.goHome()
442		case "tab":
443			m.switchTab((m.activeTab + 1) % tabCount)
444			cmd := m.enterTab()
445			return m, cmd
446		case "shift+tab":
447			m.switchTab((m.activeTab + tabCount - 1) % tabCount)
448			cmd := m.enterTab()
449			return m, cmd
450		// 1-4 jumped straight to a tab. They were the application's only numeric
451		// bindings, and an exception in a single view is precisely what §3.26
452		// dismantles — tab reaches all four.
453		case "c", "h", "m", "l":
454			return m.toggleSeverity(msg.String())
455		case pssFilterKey:
456			return m.togglePSS()
457		case keymap.Exclude:
458			return m.handleIgnoreSecret()
459		case openPipelineKey:
460			return m.openResolvedPipeline()
461		case keymap.Scan:
462			// Off the Remediation tab this refuses, with the reason (Rule 130).
463			return m.scanCandidates()
464		case writeRemediationKey:
465			// One key, one verb — write the file — applied to whichever tab's
466			// object. The Remediation tab writes a base image, the
467			// Misconfigurations tab a built-in fix; anywhere else the refusal says
468			// which tab it belongs to (Rule 130).
469			if m.activeTab == TabMisconfig {
470				return m.prepareMisconfigFix()
471			}
472			return m.prepareRemediationWrite()
473		}
474		// `.` is the sort again, and the search and the severity tokens are the
475		// table's (Rule 136).
476		return m, m.findingsTable.Update(msg)
477	}
478	
479	// toggleSeverity flips one severity token. Cumulative: c and h together ask for
480	// "CRITICAL or HIGH", which is the question a threshold cycle could not put.
481	func (m Model) toggleSeverity(key string) (tea.Model, tea.Cmd) {
482		label := map[string]string{"c": "critical", "h": "high", "m": "medium", "l": "low"}[key]
483		m.findingsTable.SetTokenActive(label, !m.findingsTable.IsTokenActive(label))
484		m.findingsTable.GotoTop()
485		return m, nil
486	}
487	
488	// resizeFindings lays the findings table out. Every tab gets the whole height:
489	// the CI tab used to give two rows to a score line above the table, and losing
490	// two findings on one tab out of five — for a letter the inventory already
491	// carries per target — was not worth the jump on every tab switch.
492	func (m *Model) resizeFindings() {
493		// The File column belongs to the Misconfigurations tab: the same rule
494		// there can fire in many files, and nowhere else it says nothing more than
495		// the title. Done here, with the size, so a tab switch and a resize cannot
496		// disagree.
497		m.findingsTable.SetColumnHidden(fileColumn, m.activeTab != TabMisconfig)
498		m.findingsTable.Resize(m.width, max(m.height, 5))
499		m.remediation.table.Resize(m.width, max(m.height, 5))
500	}

17	// View is the Bubble Tea v2 face of Render: the content only. The terminal
18	// state (alternate screen, colours) belongs to whoever owns the program.
19	func (m Model) View() tea.View { return tea.NewView(m.Render()) }
20	
21	// Render renders the UI
22	func (m Model) Render() string {
23		// Show whichever modal is active (Rule 112: modals confirm, forms fill the
24		// viewport).
25		if modal := m.modalView(); modal != "" {
26			return lipgloss.Place(
27				m.width, m.height,
28				lipgloss.Center, lipgloss.Center,
29				modal,
30				lipgloss.WithWhitespaceStyle(lipgloss.NewStyle().Background(theme.ColorBackground)),
31			)
32		}
33	
34		switch m.state {
35		case StateInventory:
36			return m.renderInventoryView()
37		case StateResults:
38			return m.renderResultsView()
39		case StateDetails:
40			return m.renderDetailsView()
41		}
42		return ""
43	}
44	
45	// renderResultsView renders the results summary
46	func (m Model) renderResultsView() string {
47		if m.result == nil {
48			return "No results"
49		}
50	
51		// A stage that failed is **not** rendered here. It goes to the log, and the
52		// footer says to look there (Rule 128).
53		//
54		// It used to be a panel that replaced the whole table whenever
55		// Result.Errors was non-empty, on the stated grounds that a failed scan has
56		// no partial results to browse. That held while an error meant nothing had
57		// run; it stopped holding the day a stage could fail beside three that
58		// succeeded, and a plumber failure then took every CVE and every secret
59		// down with it. Folding it to a banner above the table only moved the
60		// problem — five tabs, permanently, for a message read once — and a tool's
61		// stderr reformatted for a viewport is what a log is for.
62		//
63		// Nothing is lost by it: internal/scan logs every stage failure at the
64		// point it records one, which it did not do before. The only copy of the
65		// reason used to be on screen.
66		//
67		// The grade had a line of its own above the table on the CI tab, and it is
68		// gone: it cost that tab two of its rows — the line and its blank — on
69		// every open, to state a letter the inventory's own CI column carries per
70		// target. A tab that shows fewer findings than its four neighbours, for a
71		// value already on the previous screen, is not a trade worth making.
72		if m.activeTab == TabRemediation {
73			return m.remediation.table.View()
74		}
75		return m.findingsTable.View()
76	}
77	
78	// GetFooterHeight returns the footer height for this view (Rule 124).
79	func (m Model) GetFooterHeight() int {
80		height := 2 // empty line + info line
81		if m.showsResultTabs() {
82			height = 3 // tab bar + empty line + info line
83		}
84		if bar := m.activeFilterBar(); bar != nil {
85			height += bar.ExtraHeight() // Rule 136
86		}
87		return height
88	}
89	
90	// RenderFooter returns the footer content rendered below the viewport (Rule 124).
91	//
92	// The bar comes first whatever the state, because its top edge *is* the
93	// viewport's bottom border (Rule 136) — the same order oci_resources uses for
94	// the one bar it draws above a tab bar.
95	//
96	// It is resolved through activeFilterBar, like the height. The results branch
97	// drew no bar at all while GetFooterHeight counted one, so the router took two
98	// lines off the viewport and nothing filled them: the table's bottom border
99	// climbed the moment a severity token went on, and the tokens the user had just
100	// switched on were nowhere on screen.
101	func (m Model) RenderFooter(width int) string {
102		var parts []string
103		if bar := m.activeFilterBar(); bar != nil {
104			parts = append(parts, bar.View())
105		}
106		if m.showsResultTabs() {
107			parts = append(parts, theme.PadWithBg(theme.Bg(" ")+m.renderTabs(), width))
108		}
109		parts = append(parts, theme.EmptyLineBg(width), m.renderInfoLine(width))
110		return strings.Join(parts, "\n")
111	}
112	
113	// modalView renders whichever modal is open, or "" when none is.
114	func (m Model) modalView() string {
115		switch {
116		case m.confirmModal != nil:
117			return m.confirmModal.View()
118		case m.scanAllModal != nil:
119			return m.scanAllModal.View()
120		}
121		return ""
122	}
123	
124	// activeFilterBar is the bar of whichever table is on screen, or nil when the
125	// state has no table. One resolution rather than three, so GetFooterHeight and
126	// RenderFooter cannot disagree about whether the bar is there — which is the
127	// one way to make Rule 124's arithmetic wrong by a line.
128	func (m Model) activeFilterBar() *sharedcomponents.FilterBar {
129		var bar *sharedcomponents.FilterBar
130		switch {
131		case m.state == StateInventory:
132			bar = m.inventory.FilterBar()
133		case m.showsResultTabs() && m.activeTab != TabRemediation:
134			// The Remediation tab has a table of its own and no filter: the bar
135			// belongs to the findings table behind it.
136			bar = m.findingsTable.FilterBar()
137		}
138		if bar == nil || !bar.IsVisible() {
139			return nil
140		}
141		return bar
142	}
143	
144	// showsResultTabs reports whether the findings tab bar is on screen.
145	//
146	// A failed stage no longer takes it away, because nothing replaces the table
147	// any more: the tabs are what the results state is browsed with, and an empty
148	// one is an honest answer — the footer says which stage failed and where to
149	// read why.
150	func (m Model) showsResultTabs() bool {
151		return m.state == StateResults && m.result != nil
152	}
153	
154	// renderInfoLine is the footer's message line, always rendered even when empty
155	// (Rule 124). The message expires on its own after three seconds (Rule 128).
156	func (m Model) renderInfoLine(width int) string {
157		return m.footer.View(width, m.status())
158	}
159	
160	// status is what the footer says when no message is in flight.
161	//
162	// A stage that failed is a **state** of the result rather than an event: it is
163	// true for as long as the result is on screen, and a message would expire after
164	// three seconds — the distinction Rule 128 draws between the two. It carries
165	// the error level, because that is what happened, and it names the stages so
166	// the log can be searched for them.
167	func (m Model) status() sharedcomponents.Status {
168		if m.state == StateInventory {
169			return m.inventoryStatus()
170		}
171		// Which lines of a long detail are on screen: a state of the screen, derived
172		// here and never stored, so no timer can take it away (Rule 128).
173		if m.state == StateDetails {
174			if status, ok := m.verifyingStatus(); ok {
175				return status
176			}
177			if m.previewingStatus() {
178				return sharedcomponents.Status{Text: preparingFooter, Activity: true}
179			}
180			vp := m.detailsViewport
181			return sharedcomponents.Status{Text: scrollPosition(vp.YOffset(), vp.VisibleLineCount(), vp.TotalLineCount())}
182		}
183		// Ahead of the failed stages below: on this tab what is happening now is
184		// what the footer is for, and a stage that failed still shows on the others.
185		if status, ok := m.remediationStatus(); ok {
186			return status
187		}
188		if m.state != StateResults || m.result == nil || len(m.result.Errors) == 0 {
189			return sharedcomponents.Status{}
190		}
191		return sharedcomponents.Status{
192			Text:  failedStages(m.result.Errors) + " — check logs",
193			Level: sharedcomponents.LevelError,
194		}
195	}
196	
197	// inventoryStatus is the inventory footer: the selected row's own activity
198	// (its detail), composed with the batch progress or, while the caches are
199	// read, the load text. The load no longer hides the row: a failed row still
200	// says so under a ctrl+r.
201	func (m Model) inventoryStatus() sharedcomponents.Status {
202		st := sharedcomponents.Status{Text: sharedcomponents.JobsStatusLine(m.jobs, command.ViewSecurity)}
203		if m.inventoryLoading {
204			st.Text = "Loading scan inventory..."
205		}
206		moving := false
207		if row, ok := m.inventory.Selected(); ok {
208			a := m.rowActivity(row)
209			st.Detail = a.Detail
210			moving = a.State == indicator.Running || a.State == indicator.Queued
211		}
212		// The load and jobs work share the one activity dot; only a detail whose dot
213		// moves replaces it (a failed row's is fixed).
214		st.Activity = m.inventoryLoading ||
215			len(jobs.Unfinished(m.jobs)) > 0 && (!moving || st.Detail.IsZero())
216		return st
217	}
218	
219	// failedStages names what failed, reading the "<stage>: <reason>" that
220	// scan.recordStageError writes. The reason stays in the log: a footer is one
221	// line, and a tool's stderr is not.
222	func failedStages(errs []string) string {
223		stages := make([]string, 0, len(errs))
224		for _, e := range errs {
225			stage := e
226			if idx := strings.Index(e, ": "); idx != -1 {
227				stage = e[:idx]
228			}
229			stages = append(stages, stage)
230		}
231		return strings.Join(stages, ", ") + " failed"
232	}
233	
234	// renderTabs renders the tab bar
235	func (m Model) renderTabs() string {
236		cve, secrets, licenses, misconfigs, ci := m.countFindingsByTab()
237	
238		return theme.RenderTabs([]theme.TabItem{
239			{Label: fmt.Sprintf("CVE (%d)", cve)},
240			{Label: fmt.Sprintf("Secrets (%d)", secrets)},
241			{Label: fmt.Sprintf("Licenses (%d)", licenses)},
242			{Label: fmt.Sprintf("Misconfig (%d)", misconfigs)},
243			// The count, like its four neighbours — not the letter. A letter in a
244			// column of counts would break the only thing the tab bar keeps
245			// aligned, and the grade already has a line of its own below.
246			{Label: fmt.Sprintf("CI (%d)", ci)},
247			{Label: m.remediationTabLabel()},
248		}, m.activeTab)
249	}

17	func (m Model) GetShortcuts() shortcut.Shortcuts {
18		switch m.state {
19		case StateInventory:
20			return m.inventoryShortcuts()
21		case StateResults:
22			return m.resultsShortcuts()
23		case StateDetails:
24			return m.detailsShortcuts()
25		}
26		return nil

28	
29	// detailsShortcuts is the detail's column: the same six keys for every finding,
30	// each greyed when it has nothing to act on (Rule 130). Every availability is
31	// computed from the finding on screen alone, so the header reads no file. The
32	// descriptions are at most ten cells: the column is 19 cells wide at 80 columns
33	// and `<ctrl+o>` takes nine of them.
34	func (m Model) detailsShortcuts() shortcut.Shortcuts {
35		// A finding with no published reference is the same screen as one with three,
36		// so W is greyed rather than dropped. keymap.Web is what handleDetailsState
37		// binds: a key advertised under another name would do nothing.
38		f := m.selectedFinding
39		return []shortcut.Shortcut{
40			{Key: "esc", Description: "Back"},
41			{Key: keymap.Web, Description: "Open ref", Disabled: f == nil || len(f.References) == 0},
42			{Key: "enter", Description: "Open file", Disabled: !m.canOpenFindingFile().Enabled()},
43			{Key: writeRemediationKey, Description: "Apply fix", Disabled: !m.canFixMisconfig().Enabled()},
44			{Key: keymap.Copy, Description: "Copy cmd", Disabled: !m.canCopyFixCommand().Enabled()},
45			{Key: keymap.Exclude, Description: "Exclude", Disabled: !m.canExclude().Enabled()},
46		}
47	}
48	
49	// resultsShortcuts advertises the findings table's own keys.
50	//
51	// The four severity toggles were bound and unadvertised — a user had to open
52	// the help to learn the view filtered at all — and `.` was offered on three
53	// tabs out of four, from back when it cycled the severity floor. It is the sort
54	// now (Rule 111), so it applies wherever there is a table.
55	//
56	// While the search has the keyboard, everything else is a character: listing
57	// keys that no longer do what they say is worse than listing nothing, so only
58	// the two that end the search are shown. Same shape as the ports view.
59	func (m Model) resultsShortcuts() shortcut.Shortcuts {
60		if m.findingsTable.InEditMode() {
61			return shortcut.Shortcuts{{Key: "enter/esc", Description: "Confirm / Cancel search"}}
62		}
63		// X is greyed rather than dropped (Rule 130): a tab is not a different
64		// screen, and the entry used to appear and disappear as the cursor crossed
65		// a Trivy secret in a list holding both tools' findings.
66		// The Remediation tab has a table of its own: what filters and sorts the
67		// findings does not reach it, so those keys are greyed there and S — which
68		// means nothing on the four tabs of findings — is the one that lights up.
69		notFindings := m.activeTab == TabRemediation
70		// Enter opens the selected finding, or on the Remediation tab the diff of the
71		// chosen bases: one key, the same place in the column, a different verb.
72		enter := shortcut.Shortcut{Key: "enter", Description: "Details", Disabled: !m.canOpenFinding().Enabled()}
73		if notFindings {
74			enter = shortcut.Shortcut{Key: "enter", Description: "Show diff", Disabled: !m.canPreviewRemediation().Enabled()}
75		}
76		// ctrl+o is one key with one verb — write the file — and the object it
77		// writes is the tab's. The label changes with it so the column never
78		// offers "Write Dockerfile" on a tab holding a Kubernetes manifest.

145	// GetHeaderInfo returns the key-value info for the header: the context, one
146	// count, and in the results how much of it is fixable.
147	//
148	// It used to carry seven fields in the results state, which is exactly the
149	// number buildInfoLines renders — an eighth would have been dropped in silence.
150	// Most of them had stopped earning their line:
151	//
152	//   - Trivy and Gitleaks versions answered "can I scan?", which the dashboard
153	//     already answers from shared.State.Tools, and which an inventory of past
154	//     scans is not about.
155	//   - Filter showed the severity filter, permanently reading ALL, and meaning
156	//     nothing on the Secrets tab or in the details.
157	//   - Secrets and Licenses duplicated the tab bar, which renders the same two
158	//     numbers a line below.
159	//
160	// Fixable came back on its own merits: it is the one figure that says what can
161	// be done, which none of the removed ones did.
162	//
163	// The context is what replaced them, and it is the one thing that was missing:
164	// the scan caches are scoped to a context, so the same inventory rows mean
165	// different things in two of them and look identical.
166	func (m Model) GetHeaderInfo(context string) []shortcut.HeaderInfo {
167		info := []shortcut.HeaderInfo{
168			{Key: "Context", Value: context, Style: theme.HeaderValueStyle},
169		}
170		if key, value, ok := m.headerCount(); ok {
171			info = append(info, shortcut.HeaderInfo{Key: key, Value: value, Style: theme.HeaderValueStyle})
172		}
173		if pss, ok := m.pssHeader(); ok {
174			info = append(info, pss)
175		}
176		if value, style, ok := m.headerFixable(); ok {
177			info = append(info, shortcut.HeaderInfo{Key: "Fixable", Value: value, Style: style})
178		}
179		if value, ok := m.headerUnrendered(); ok {
180			info = append(info, shortcut.HeaderInfo{Key: "Not rendered", Value: value, Style: theme.HeaderValueStyle})
181		}
182		if sig, ok := m.signatureHeader(); ok {
183			info = append(info, sig)
184		}
185		return info
186	}
